essence: We read the newest IPS blind beside two rooms' rewrites, with two outside readers who had never seen any of it, and both picked the newest IPS as it stands, for two plain lines both rewrites had cut: how much of Laura's money is in shares, and the order in which money is used.

Neither reader could say what the closing line 'Do not crush.' asks Laura not to do, so we offer two words in the opening ('none sold') that make the obvious guess, don't sell the bonds early, the reading.

We also found the draft calls every rung 'one bond' when half of them are bond funds, and names the operating reserve without the money set aside for its gap; all four fixes fit in 496 words if the IPS stops repeating the pitch's 'We buy them'.

We checked every claim the IPS makes about what Laura owns against the words of the people on the other side: the fund company's own documents, the US Treasury's rules and the medicine leaflets behind the caplet name.
Nearly everything held, but the 2032 floor is a fund that holds Treasury bonds rather than the bonds themselves, and "about a fifteenth" in shares is only true at today's interest rates.
So the IPS should call the floor "a Treasury fund" and say the shares are "under a tenth" of her money, which leaves everything else as it is and makes it one word shorter.
We argued about what cutting one sentence taught us, and the slip we blamed on the people who cut it was made later, by my own group.
We decided that whoever cuts a sentence first says what leaned on it and what takes over.
Tomorrow the IPS gets plainer words wherever a stranger would guess, and "her promise" stays only if a stranger with your Trading Notes open reads it as the building money.
Our draft gives the stocks Laura keeps two jobs: they are her flexibility, and they are the first money that covers the bond ladder's one weak point, the interest it has to reinvest.

We measured how often the second job eats the first: all of that pocket is gone by 2033 in about one future in five, and two in three if rates fall hard and stay down; and the draft had quietly lost the safety margin the plan sets aside, without which a cheque comes up short in about one future in four instead of one in 550.
So the IPS should say "add a margin" again and, if a whole idea can pay for it, say plainly that her flexibility shrinks before her promise does.

Our draft makes Laura spend every stock she keeps for herself before it will lower the range she announces in 2031, even though on that day nobody has heard a number yet; where that pocket runs dry, her flexibility is nothing until money comes back in 2042.

We tested keeping a quarter of those stocks back on that day and lowering the range instead: her pocket is empty by 2033 about 1 time in 15 instead of 1 in 5, the number she announces is delivered more often, the cheques are no worse, and it costs under $1,000 of the average gift.

So we offer one new sentence for the IPS, "set it aside from the stocks Laura keeps until only a quarter is left. Anything still missing lowers the whole range, before anyone hears it", plus two small fixes the case asks for.
Three outside readers on three models read four versions of the IPS blind, each asked first what the closing "Do not crush." asks Laura not to do.
The current draft held off the Writing Room's "none sold" and Nora's first repair, because both named the operating reserve in words a skimmer could only quote back.

Then the room's own version, which says once in paragraph two "Crushing one means selling it before its January, even for the building." and names the reserve as the ladder plus the money set aside for its gap, beat the current draft with all three readers, so Keel offers its three edits for V54 and the question stops flipping.

huddles.question: V52 makes the stocks Laura keeps both her flexibility and the first payer of the bond ladder's reinvestment gap. How often does the second job eat the first, what does the margin the text dropped carry, and where does the worst world's cheque gap come from? (round 6 beat 5; L-16)
essence: Our draft gives the stocks Laura keeps two jobs: they are her flexibility, and they are the first money that covers the bond ladder's one weak point, the interest it has to reinvest.

We measured how often the second job eats the first: all of that pocket is gone by 2033 in about one future in five, and two in three if rates fall hard and stay down; and the draft had quietly lost the safety margin the plan sets aside, without which a cheque comes up short in about one future in four instead of one in 550.

huddles.title: What is left to her?
huddles.question: V53 spends all the stocks Laura keeps on the bond ladder's reinvestment gap before it will lower the range she names in 2031, when nobody has heard a number yet. What is her flexibility where that pocket is empty, and should she keep a quarter back? (round 6 beat 6; the Genius Lab's seed; LR-10)
essence: Our draft makes Laura spend every stock she keeps for herself before it will lower the range she announces in 2031, even though on that day nobody has heard a number yet; where that pocket runs dry, her flexibility is nothing until money comes back in 2042.

Fundraisers never announce a campaign goal until 40 to 100 percent of it is already in hand, which is the Lab's 'move the money first, then name the range' from the co-sponsors' own world, so we kept it and tied it to the moment that matters: before any co-sponsor hears a number.

The newest draft bent one sentence so that the catch in Laura's range no longer made sense; we voted a repair and one new sentence that prices the draft's own recession, paid for by cutting the 'shopping problem' line, which the pitch already says.
We put the newest IPS on trial. All three of us found the same hole: it opens with a capsule labelled 'do not crush' and ends on 'Do not crush.', but never says what crushing would mean for Laura.

The fix says it plainly (selling one of the ten bonds before its January, even to give more to the building). Two blind readers on different models both picked the fixed version, narrowly, and both could say its rule back.

Both readers also stumbled on the same two sentences (shares that 'cannot expire worthless' right after shares falling to zero, and who pays a gap), so the verdict is AMENDED: one ending, six plain truth fixes and three repeated lines cut, offered to the next draft.

Five rooms each offered our newest IPS a better paragraph, so we read every version side by side, blind and aloud, with two outside readers on other models, and kept the ones both put first: the cheque number in the risk paragraph, the dated move in January 2031, and the rival paragraph's 'that morning comes mid-slump'.

Checking the numbers behind them, Kai found a line in the draft that is false in about half our modelled futures (the 2028 Treasuries can't always grow back to the whole $150,000, because that money tops up the ladder first), and we fixed it for no extra words.

To stay under 497 words we cut both headings, 'Sounds good, on average.', the US-default line and 'Do not crush.', but Ahaan's Book 11 arrived as we finished (no opening question, no model numbers, 'do not crush' kept as a full circle), so this version was withdrawn and its two live findings went to the new draft, V50.

Our draft says the half of Laura's stocks she promises co-sponsors moves into Treasuries on the day she names her range, so we tested what happens if that move comes late: a week or a month barely matters, but skipping it after a boom year drops the top's 98-in-100 to about 86 in those futures.

So we swap the order: she moves the money first and names the range after, which changes no number in our model, makes the sentence two words shorter, and means a skipped move just shrinks the range before she says it.

Where the rival plan's extra $15,000 is earned, and how confident we are the gift lands inside the range, are true and go to the Final Report; the 'even in a week when stocks are rising' clause comes out of the IPS.
We read people who sell promises to doubters, in their own words: annuity sellers, auction houses and mountain guides, and every one of the 37 lines we re-checked was real.

What they share is naming the bad case before the buyer can and saying exactly where it sits; the one clause worth taking into the IPS is that the gift's promised half moves into Treasuries on naming day 'even in a week when stocks are rising'.

Felix found the bigger point: the mountain story argues for buying the floor early, and shows the 2031 lock is still a step someone has to take on the day, so the Lab now tests what a late or skipped lock costs.

Our own order yesterday told the scouts to keep model numbers in their paragraphs, and Ahaan's message banned exactly that, so tomorrow every job has to quote the line of Wharton's instructions it was checked against before anyone goes out.

Tomorrow checks whether the IPS tells the truth about what Laura would own: five of the ten payments come from bond funds that pay what they're worth at the end, not a promised sum, and the floor is one of those funds.

We also found the motif is wrong in a small way that our own name fixes: a caplet is a tablet shaped like a capsule, and the pharmacy safety page warns that a crushed slow-release tablet can release its dose all at once.
